title: How I got highlighted by OpenAI in their pretraining competition
description: Two small ideas: share vocabulary across capitalization, and let learning survive the end of a document.
markdown:
OpenAI [highlighted my CaseOps tokenizer](https://openai.com/index/what-parameter-golf-taught-us/) in its Parameter Golf write-up. It started with a simple question: why should a tiny language model spend vocabulary entries learning that “apple,” “Apple,” and “APPLE” are related?

[Parameter Golf](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf) gave us **16 MB for the model artifact, ten minutes to train on eight H100s, and ten minutes to evaluate**. The score was bits per byte on held-out text: how many bits the model needed to predict each byte. Lower was better.

I worked on **CaseOps**, a tokenizer that shares vocabulary across capitalization patterns, and **phased test-time training**, which carries learning from one evaluation document into the next.

## CaseOps: learn the word once

A case-sensitive tokenizer can give “apple,” “Apple,” and “APPLE” different vocabulary entries or different subword splits. With only 8,192 entries, that duplication is expensive.

CaseOps separates spelling from capitalization:

<!--CASEOPS_SHARING-->

The same lowercase pieces work in all three cases. Capitalization becomes a reusable operation the model can apply to any word.

<!--CASEOPS_DEMO-->

The implementation is small: transform the text before BPE tokenization, then undo the transform when decoding. Title case and all caps each need one operator. Mixed case uses an operator that capitalizes the next letter; an escape operator handles literal control characters. Non-ASCII characters pass through unchanged.

The transformer itself doesn't change. We're giving it a representation where related words already share their spelling, instead of asking it to discover that relationship from scratch.

### The detail that makes the score meaningful

Adding capitalization operators changes the length of the encoded text. If we divided the loss by that new byte count, we could make the score look better just by making the representation longer.

So the exporter saves **original byte counts alongside the tokens**. The evaluator divides by those counts. The model pays to predict every capitalization operator, and the denominator still measures the text we started with.

My [submission](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1729) combined CaseOps with a late weight-decay taper on the existing phased-TTT stack: **1.06780 bits per byte**, averaged over three seeds, in **15.94 MB**. The [code and tokenizer details are here](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/tree/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper).

## Phased TTT: let learning survive the document

The competition allowed the model to learn from text **after scoring it**, to help predict what came next. Earlier scores stayed fixed.

[Samacqua's evaluator](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1530) already used that within each document: score a chunk, train a small LoRA adapter on it, then predict the next chunk. At the document boundary, reset the adapter.

That gives the model a useful short-term memory. But every new document starts from the same base model. My addition was a second, slower learning loop: **update the base model using completed documents, so later documents inherit what it learned.**

<!--TTT_DIAGRAM-->

My [first implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1610) paused after 2,000 completed documents, ran distributed SGD on that already-scored prefix, then resumed evaluation. Each new document still got a fresh local adapter, now on top of an improved base.

### Why pause instead of learning continuously?

I first tried mixing local and global updates more continuously. Synchronizing the shared model across GPUs kept getting in the way of the local work.

Phases made the coordination simple: **score in parallel, pause for a shared training phase, then go back to scoring**. It also makes the information flow obvious. Global training only sees documents whose scores are already recorded.

With pretraining unchanged, the [three-seed mean](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-13_VarLenAttn_PhasingTTT2000/README.md) improved from **1.07336 → 1.07281 bits per byte**, staying within the evaluation budget. The evaluation still fit within the time limit.

[Dexhunter extended it to three phases](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1626), and I built CaseOps on top of that version.

title: Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API
description: A hidden optimizer, a programmable LoRA adapter, and a symmetry trick that made the update rule fall out.
markdown:
Thinking Machines released DiMuon, a LoRA optimizer available through [Tinker](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/optimizers/), without publishing its update equations. We tried to recover them using only the API.

We ended up with a local reconstruction that replayed **four batches of SST2 gradients with every recovered FP16 polar-output value matching**. That experiment used rank-one LoRA on Qwen3-8B's output projection, with gradients measured at Tinker's weights.

## The rule: scale, polar, scale again

[Muon](https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/) takes a momentum matrix and approximately makes its nonzero singular values equal. This stops the largest singular direction from dominating the update.

The interesting addition in DiMuon is a **row-and-column sandwich**. The previous momentum determines which rows and columns to scale. Apply that scaling before Muon's polar transform, then apply it again afterward.

<!--DIMUON_SANDWICH-->

Rows and columns with stronger old momentum get smaller multipliers. The two LoRA matrices—the wide A and tall B—get the same final update norm.

The scaling statistics are cheap to compute from the momentum the optimizer already keeps.

## The trick: turn the model into a linear system

LoRA learns a weight change **BA**: A compresses an input into a few coordinates, and B expands it back out. The original model weight stays frozen.

At initialization, **B = 0**. Put that adapter on the output projection, and the transformer supplies a fixed feature h. The trainable addition to the logits is just sBAh. From B's perspective, an eight-billion-parameter language model has become a linear system.

We could simplify the loss too. Cross-entropy contains a shared log-sum-exp term; signed token weights that sum to zero cancel it. What's left is a linear combination of logits.

Now we could construct useful gradient patterns instead of hoping ordinary text would produce them. To read those gradients back, we borrowed [Martin Marek's large-epsilon Adam trick](https://x.com/mrtnm/status/2114145574987702525): choose an invertible optimizer step, download the weights, and undo the step mathematically. Adam became our gradient meter.

## Making the unknown cancel

We wanted to know whether DiMuon scaled the matrix **after** the polar transform. But we hadn't reproduced that transform precisely yet.

So we chose a gradient that made two axes equal at its input. Symmetry forces the polar computation to treat them equally. Their common response cancels when you take the output ratio—leaving the post-scaling exposed.

<!--DIMUON_ISOLATION-->

The predicted ratio agreed with the API to about eight significant figures.

A second simple experiment explained where the scaling came from: build history with learning rate zero, then set beta to zero for the measured step. The current momentum forgets the past, yet the update still changes. The old momentum is doing a second job: choosing the row and column scaling.

## Same math, different program

The numerics turned into a second puzzle: **which way of computing the same equation matched the API?** Three details stood out.

### Rearrange the polynomial

Each polar stage applies a polynomial to the working matrix X. Here R = XᵀX, I is the identity, and a, b, c are that stage's coefficients. We initially evaluated it in expanded form. Switching to **Horner form** made the difference:

<!--DIMUON_HORNER-->

The coefficients stayed the same. The rearranged version matched all eleven of our retained numerical fingerprints.

This is a natural optimization for LoRA: X is tall and skinny, while R is only rank × rank. Folding the aX term into the small matrix avoids a separate multiply-and-add over the entire large matrix. It also changes where rounding happens. The algebra alone doesn't tell you which program ran.

### Catch an intermediate being rounded

Inside the Horner calculation, **cR gets rounded to FP16 before adding bI**. Keeping that intermediate in higher precision gives a different answer.

We made two inputs specifically to distinguish those implementations. Skipping the FP16 store missed their tiny output ratios by about **20% and 4.6%**; including it matched both to roughly **4 × 10⁻⁸** relative error.

That's a surprisingly specific thing to learn through an API. A low-precision tensor operation naturally leaves this kind of trace: the result gets stored before the next operation reads it. “More accurate” arithmetic erased the trace we were trying to reproduce.

### Let the GPU split up the work

One CPU replay still differed by **0.79%**. Native FP16 matrix products on an H100 brought that case to roughly **8 × 10⁻⁸**. The first Gram matrix differed by just one FP16 rounding step; the polynomial amplified it.

Profiling our GPU replay exposed a useful reason: **split-K**. The GPU divides a long dot product into chunks, computes them in parallel, then combines the partial sums. That helps keep it busy when the output matrix is tiny—exactly the shape LoRA produces. [cuBLAS allows those partial sums to be stored in FP16](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/12.8.0/cublas/index.html#cublasltreduction-scheme-t), adding another rounding boundary.

<!--DIMUON_SPLITK-->

We could reproduce two of our GPU execution paths by changing only the split count and partial-sum precision. That parallelization choice left a visible signature in the optimizer's output.

[Update equations and experiment details →](/reverse-engineering-dimuon/notes/) · [Replay data →](/data/dimuon-replay-2026-10-31.json)
notes:
These are the equations and measurement details behind [Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API](/reverse-engineering-dimuon/).

## The gradient-meter equations

With no clipping or weight decay, a coordinate moves by:

```math
u=-\eta\frac{g}{|g|+\epsilon},
\qquad
g=-\frac{\epsilon u}{\eta-|u|}.
```

Large epsilon avoids saturation. We repeated measurements with different epsilon values to check the recovered gradients, including their rounding.

## The complete update equations

After optional joint gradient clipping, form the current momentum:

```math
M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\widetilde G_t.
```

Compute energies from the previous momentum:

```math
e_i=\sum_j M_{t-1,ij}^2,
\qquad f_j=\sum_i M_{t-1,ij}^2.
```

Normalize each vector by its maximum, add a small ridge, and take the inverse fourth root:

```math
D_r=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{e_i}{\max_k e_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right],
```

```math
D_c=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{f_j}{\max_k f_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right].
```

Zero old momentum uses relative energies of one. The ridge keeps inactive coordinates from getting unbounded multipliers. Energy is a squared norm, so its inverse fourth root is an inverse square root of the norm.

Then:

```math
U_t=D_r\,\Phi(D_rM_tD_c)\,D_c,
\qquad \Delta\theta_t=-\eta C(r)\frac{U_t}{\|U_t\|_F}.
```

Φ includes the approximate polar computation and its input normalization. A zero direction gets a zero update. At alpha 32, tested ranks 1 through 64 followed:

```math
C(r)=\sqrt r\left(\frac r{32}\right)^{0.175}.
```

This predicted a held-out rank-16 norm to about 5.6 × 10⁻⁸ relative error. The origin of 0.175 is still a mystery.

## The polar computation we replayed

Normalize the preconditioned momentum and store it in FP16:

```math
X=\operatorname{round}_{\mathrm{FP16}}\left(
\frac{D_rM_tD_c}{1.01\max(\|D_rM_tD_c\|_F,10^{-7})}
\right).
```

For a tall matrix, form the small Gram matrix R = XᵀX and apply a stage:

```math
X\leftarrow X\left[aI+R(bI+cR)\right].
```

The coefficients change each stage. Wide matrices use the transposed construction. The intermediate stores matter, as does how the GPU reduces each matrix product.

## Experiment and measurement details

The ordinary steps use learning rate 0.001. Subtracting two nearly equal exported weights loses precision, so we also measure updates with the learning rate enlarged to 16. That changes the readout gain while keeping the optimizer state and gradient fixed.

With that readout, relative update errors were 7.6 × 10⁻⁸ to 1.21 × 10⁻⁷. At the ordinary learning rate, errors in the subtracted updates range from roughly 2 × 10⁻⁶ to 2.4 × 10⁻⁵; the accumulated local weights differ from the hosted weights by at most 9.3 × 10⁻¹⁰. The replay uses measured gradients at the hosted weights; it does not recompute them with a separate local language model. Other experiments include an unresolved 0.81% discrepancy in a rank-two B continuation and 1.14% RMS across historical A updates. The [replay data](/data/dimuon-replay-2026-10-31.json) covers the four-step rank-one experiment.

title: Two NanoGPT experiments: attention gradients and table votes
description: Skipping some attention backward work, and letting an n-gram table vote on the answer.
markdown:
I've been playing with [modded-nanogpt](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt), where the short track asks how quickly you can train a language model to a target validation loss. Two things I tried ended up being interesting for pretty different reasons: one cuts out work in attention's backward pass, and the other gives a lookup table a direct say in the model's predictions.

Both are open submissions: [approximate backward](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/371) and [table voting](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/399). They build on different versions of the track, so their timings aren't directly comparable.

## How much attention needs a backward pass?

An attention head can look back over a long window, but it doesn't necessarily spread its attention evenly across that window. If most of the useful signal is concentrated nearby, maybe we can leave the forward pass alone and skip some distant work when calculating gradients.

That's what I tried in [#371](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/371). For eligible heads, I compared backward windows of 64, 128, and 256 tokens with the original backward pass at two training steps. A head got the cheapest window whose query, key, and value gradients each had at most 0.2 relative L2 error on both steps and every rank. If none passed, it kept the full window.

The forward pass still sees the original window. In the backward pass, the kernel skips distant tiles while retaining the original softmax normalization; it doesn't renormalize the attention that remains. So this is a biased approximation, and attention being sharp isn't by itself a guarantee that the gradient will be close. The comparison against the actual gradients is what decides which heads get shortened.

The same submission also approximates the language-model head's weight gradient: it samples one row in four for the dense positive part and scales that contribution up, while accumulating the sparse target entries separately. The input gradient remains intact. Both approximations are used for part of training, and the last 87 updates use the original backward pass.

Together, on the same 8×H100 node, the modified run averaged **39.583 seconds** over 12 runs versus **40.342 seconds** over six baseline runs, with mean validation loss of **3.278705** versus **3.279000**. That's a 1.88% time saving for the combined changes, including calibration. The comparison doesn't isolate how much each approximation contributed.

## Let the lookup table vote

The track has since taken a pretty dramatic turn. [Herman Brunborg's #367](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/367) builds a huge, lossy n-gram lookup table on the CPU in parallel with training. It looks for matching contexts in training data and gives the transformer hints about what came next. In that submission, the table covers 37 billion tokens, and the reported training time drops from around 40 seconds to 6.7 seconds on the comparison machine.

That got me wondering how much of the table the network actually learns to use during such a short training run. The model gets the matches as input, but it still has to learn what to do with them. If it underuses a useful match, there's a very old-fashioned thing to try: count what followed that context and mix those counts directly into the answer.

In [#399](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/399), the table gets a vote at validation. For the target token, the update is:

```text
voted probability = (target count + k × network probability) / (total count + k)
```

Here `k` controls how much weight the network gets relative to the observed counts. A context with no match leaves the probability alone. I apply this successively for match lengths 6, 10, and 20, shortest first. The three weights were chosen once on a separate training shard that the table doesn't cover. There is no extra table, training, or backward pass for the vote.

On seven seeds, the network alone averaged **3.2933** validation loss; with the vote, it averaged **3.2737**. The experiment used 526 training steps and a table covering 36.1 billion tokens, down from 540 steps and 37 billion in the reference setup. Since training and table construction run concurrently, that is roughly 2.5% less of each. These runs were on one H100, simulating the eight ranks in sequence, so that wall-clock saving is an estimate rather than a direct eight-GPU timing.

The result is consistent with the model leaving useful information in the table, though it doesn't prove exactly why the direct vote helps. I like that a smoothed n-gram count can still improve the final prediction even when the transformer has already seen the retrieval hints.
